title: Quapaw — the "downstream people" of the Ohio Valley
summary: The Quapaw, a Dhegiha Siouan nation, keep an oral tradition of a homeland in the Ohio River valley before settling near the mouth of the Arkansas River.
bodyMarkdown:
Some of Kentucky's oldest stories are kept far from Kentucky. The [Quapaw](https://grokipedia.com/page/Quapaw) call themselves Ugaxpa, often translated "downstream people." They are a Dhegiha Siouan nation. They share that language family and an old migration tradition with the Osage, Omaha, Ponca, and Kansa.

In that tradition, the Dhegiha peoples once lived together in the Ohio Valley. At some point they moved west. When the group reached the Mississippi, the people split. Those who turned upstream became the ancestors of the Omaha, Ponca, Osage, and Kansa. Those who went downstream became the Quapaw.

Scholars still debate when this happened and how far east the homeland reached. Some link it to the end of Mississippian life in the Ohio Valley. Others see the story as a broader memory of movement. The [Osage memory of the Ohio Valley](/stories/osage-memory-of-the-ohio-valley/) tells the upstream side of the same story.

The Quapaw settled in four villages near where the Arkansas meets the Mississippi: Kappa, Tongigua, Tourima, and Osotouy. They farmed, hunted, and traded. In 1673 the French explorers Marquette and Jolliet reached them, and the Quapaw welcomed them with the calumet pipe.

In 1686 the French built Arkansas Post near Osotouy. The Quapaw became close allies of France and traded furs for guns and goods. But European diseases cut their numbers badly.

The French name for them, spoken through other nations, gave the river its name, and later the state. Arkansas is a Quapaw story on the map.

After the Louisiana Purchase, American pressure grew. In treaties of 1818 and 1824 the Quapaw gave up nearly all their Arkansas lands. By 1834 they had been removed to what is now northeastern Oklahoma.

Their story ties Kentucky into a much wider world. The Ohio Valley was not a dead end but a homeland that people remembered as they moved across the continent. The [Mosopelea and Ofo](/stories/mosopelea-ofo-the-ohio-valley/) carried a similar memory south.

## Kentucky today

The federally recognized Quapaw Nation is based in Ottawa County, Oklahoma, where it keeps its language, clans, and annual powwow. There is no public Quapaw site in Kentucky. Their tie to this land lives in the tradition they still tell.
